Compares; secondary: Proposes an evaluation method — effect of target programming language (Python, Java, Rust, OCaml) on output-token cost and behaviour of one agent scaffold (mini-swe-agent) with five models on MiniLCB (100 LiveCodeBench v6 problems, 2,000 trajectories), controlling for problem difficulty with mixed-effects models; introduces trajectory analysis by re-executing every intermediate solution snapshot and labelling snapshot spans with a 12-label taxonomy

No SDD approach. Agent: mini-swe-agent (version not stated) with a fixed competitive-programming prompt. Models: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (local, vLLM, FP8), Gemma-4-26B-A4B (local, vLLM), GLM-5.2 (Hugging Face Inference API), GPT-5.5 (medium reasoning), Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (reasoning, 10K budget); reasoning enabled for all

Agent loop: read problem -> write solution -> run ./test.sh -> revise -> submit with sentinel when tests pass; limits 40 turns, 600 s wall clock, 256 MB memory, 10 s per test. Analysis: re-execute every intermediate solution snapshot, classify transitions (breakthrough, stay, improved, regressed, churn, broke, stuck), label spans with GPT5-Mini plus manual review

Benchmark MiniLCB, mini-swe-agent for all, one trajectory per problem and language. Values per language Python/Java/Rust/OCaml: ever-solved; median output tokens; token-cost ratio vs Python (95% CI) (Tables 2, 5, 17). (1) mini-swe-agent + Gemma-4-26B-A4B: 84/82/86/62%; 11,099/11,552/15,014/23,097; Java 0.85x (p = 0.114), Rust 1.07x (p = 0.480), OCaml 1.44x [1.18, 1.75] p < 0.001. (2) + Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: 84/79/84/77%; 2,830/3,357/4,045/8,546; Java 1.21x, Rust 1.20x (p < 0.05), OCaml 1.69x (p < 0.001). (3) + GLM-5.2: 100/97/97/99%; 861/902/1,679/1,587; Java 1.34x (p < 0.01), Rust 1.57x, OCaml 1.54x (p < 0.001). (4) + GPT-5.5: 100/99/98/97%; 643/890/834/965; Java 1.30x, Rust 1.36x, OCaml 1.30x (all p < 0.001). (5) + Claude-Sonnet-4.6: 92/96/96/95%; 1,348/1,407/1,324/1,865; Java 1.18x, Rust 1.16x, OCaml 1.28x (all p < 0.001). Final-solution accuracy only in Figure 1 (values not in the text layer; Gemma much worse on OCaml). Quality verdict and cost verdict for every configuration: no criterion stated by the authors

Tasks: 100 MiniLCB problems in 4 languages. Configurations: 5 models x 4 languages on the same mini-swe-agent scaffold, prompt template, container (Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.12.3, OCaml 5.4.1, OpenJDK 21.0.11, Rust 1.96), limits and visible tests. Baseline: Python as reference language. Acceptance: all provided tests pass (tests visible to the agent). Repetitions: one session per problem-language-model; difficulty controlled by problem random intercept. Human intervention: none. Sampling parameters stated per model

Accuracy little affected by language except Gemma on OCaml. OCaml costs significantly more output tokens than Python for all models (1.28-1.69x, p < 0.001); Java and Rust penalties model-dependent (not significant for Gemma; significant for the other four). ICC 0.73-0.97: problem difficulty dominates token variance. Gemma and Qwen keep producing hundreds to thousands of tokens after a first correct solution; Gemma on OCaml has 1,196 stuck self-loops, 92% of failed snapshots are compile errors. Error-recovery labels concentrate in OCaml. Tokens per success: OCaml most expensive for Gemma (45,390, 1.4-1.9x), narrowly for Qwen and GLM, not for GPT-5.5 or Sonnet. OCaml extra cost is not representation (median final-file tokens 272 vs Python 190, total 6,706 vs 2,548)

Yes per the authors: mixed-effects models separate language from problem difficulty, and snapshot re-execution localises behaviours (stalling, polishing passing solutions, prototyping in Python); per-problem equal-weight analyses show behaviours are not driven by a few long trajectories. Limitations stated: one scaffold, fixed prompt and limits, self-contained problems, four languages and five models

Behaviours may not generalize to other models, and language effects may change as pretraining coverage improves; single scaffold (mini-swe-agent) with fixed prompt, turn limit and timeout; self-contained problems with visible tests, so findings may not generalize to repository-scale tasks or other harnesses; inefficiency expected to be larger in less constrained settings. Gap: by-language token efficiency should be considered when benchmarking and developing multilingual agents

Values from Tables 2, 5 and 17 (p. 5, 13, 18); Figure 1 accuracy and some Table 17/18 cells not readable in the text layer. Inconsistencies: introduction says the OCaml effect is 'most pronounced ... across all models', but GPT-5.5 has Rust 1.36x > OCaml 1.30x and GLM Rust 1.57x > OCaml 1.54x; §4.1 says that for all models agents produce 'the fewest tokens when writing Python', but Table 17 medians give Sonnet Rust 1,324 < Python 1,348 and Table 2 gives Gemma Java 0.85x Python, and GLM median OCaml 1,587 < Rust 1,679 despite 'significantly more tokens when writing OCaml'; abstract says variation is 'consistent across models', while Appendix H finds OCaml is not the most expensive per success for GPT-5.5 and Sonnet. Cheating found in 2 traces (GPT-5.5, same problem). Code and data to be released upon publication (not yet available). Some code written with AI assistants. No pre-registration. Programming languages: Python, Java, Rust, OCaml (the independent variable)
